subject: Archaeology
title: Wildfire Archaeology
description: Learn Wildfire Archaeology in one minute.

hook.text: Wildfires strip away vegetation and reveal hidden sites buried beneath.

buildup.text: After fires, LiDAR finds walls and foundations that forest had concealed for centuries.

discovery.text: California's 2020 fires exposed Native American stone structures hidden under brush.

twist.text: Fire also damages sites. Intense heat cracks stone and destroys organic material.

climax.text: Archaeologists work with fire agencies to place firebreaks protecting heritage.

punchline.text: Fire reveals and destroys at once. The race is to record fast.

quiz.question: How do wildfires affect archaeological sites?
options: They only damage modern structures while preserving ancient ones
They reveal hidden sites by stripping vegetation but damage them with heat
They have no effect on stone structures underground

details.summary: Wildfires, increasingly frequent due to climate change, destroy vegetation cover and expose previously hidden archaeological sites — stone walls, earthworks, and ancient roads.
details.whyItMatters: Wildfires both reveal and threaten archaeology. Burned landscapes expose hidden sites but intense heat can damage rock art, pottery, and organic remains. Post-fire surveys are a disappearing window of archaeological opportunity.
takeaways: Wildfires remove vegetation and expose hidden archaeological sites
Post-fire LiDAR surveys reveal thousands of unknown features
Intense heat can also damage rock art and fragile deposits

faq.question: How do wildfires reveal archaeological sites?
faq.answer: Dense vegetation hides surface features. After fire removes this cover, stone foundations, terracing, and earthworks become visible from the air and ground. LiDAR surveys conducted immediately after fires, before vegetation regrows, capture features across entire burned landscapes.

faq.question: Do wildfires damage archaeological sites?
faq.answer: Yes. Intense heat can spall rock art, shatter pottery, burn organic deposits, and crack stone structures. Fire retardant chemicals can also damage surfaces. Archaeologists increasingly work with fire management agencies to identify and protect known sites during wildfire response.
